description: Discover the magical properties of magnets, magnetic and non-magnetic materials, the poles of a magnet, and how compasses use magnetic fields

slides.title: Welcome to Magnets
slides.content:
# Magnets - The Magic Pull

Have you ever played with fridge magnets or seen a crane lift huge pieces of scrap iron? They use the invisible pulling power of **magnets**!

## What You Will Learn:
- The history and discovery of magnets
- **Magnetic** vs **non-magnetic** materials
- The two **poles** of a magnet
- The rules of **attraction and repulsion**
- How a **magnetic compass** works

## The Discovery of Magnets:
- The story goes that thousands of years ago in ancient Greece, a shepherd named **Magnes** was herding his sheep.
- The metal tip of his stick and the nails in his shoes suddenly stuck to a dark rock on the mountain!
- This rock was a natural magnet, an ore of iron called **magnetite**.
- Natural magnets are pieces of stone that have the property of attracting iron.

## Artificial Magnets:
- Today, we know how to make magnets from pieces of iron. These are called **artificial magnets**.
- They come in many shapes based on how they will be used:
  - Bar magnets (rectangular block)
  - Horseshoe magnets (shaped like a 'U')
  - Cylindrical magnets
  - Button/disc magnets

> **Did You Know?** The Earth itself is a giant magnet! That is why compasses work everywhere on the planet.

slides.title: Magnetic and Non-Magnetic Materials
slides.content:
# What Do Magnets Attract?

If you take a magnet and touch it to various objects in your house, you'll find it only sticks to some things, not everything!

## 1. Magnetic Materials
- The materials which get attracted towards a magnet are magnetic.
- Magnets do not attract all metals, only specific ones!
- The most common magnetic materials are:
  - **Iron** (nails, paperclips, steel spoons)
  - **Nickel** (some coins)
  - **Cobalt**

## 2. Non-Magnetic Materials
- The materials which are NOT attracted towards a magnet are non-magnetic.
- Most things around us fall into this category.
- **Examples:**
  - Wood, plastic, rubber, glass, paper, cloth
  - **Other Metals:** Aluminum (soda cans), Copper (wires), Gold, Silver, Brass

## A Simple Separation Test:
- Imagine you accidentally dropped a box of iron nails into a sandbox.
- How would you separate them? Picking them one by one would take hours.
- Solution: Run a strong magnet through the sand! The iron nails (magnetic) will stick to the magnet, and the sand (non-magnetic) will be left behind.
- This is exactly how recycling centers separate steel cans from aluminum cans!

> **The Stainless Steel Trick:** Some stainless steel spoons are magnetic, while others are not. It depends on the exact mixture of metals used to make that specific steel!

slides.title: Poles of a Magnet
slides.content:
# Poles of a Magnet - Where the Power Lies

Is the pulling power of a magnet the same all over its surface? Let's find out!

## The Iron Filing Experiment:
1. Spread some iron filings (tiny pieces of iron) on a sheet of paper.
2. Place a bar magnet on the paper.
3. What happens? The iron filings stick to the magnet.
4. But look closely! They do not stick evenly. Most of the iron filings cling to the **two ends** of the magnet.

## What are Poles?
- The regions of a magnet where the magnetic force is the **strongest** are called the **poles**.
- Every magnet, regardless of its shape, has **two poles**.
- These poles are located near the ends of a bar magnet or at the tips of a horseshoe magnet.

## North and South:
If you suspend a bar magnet freely by a thread tied to its center, it will spin and eventually come to rest pointing in a specific direction - North and South!
- The end of the magnet that points towards the Geographic North is called the **North-seeking end** or the **North Pole (N)**.
- The end that points towards the Geographic South is called the **South-seeking end** or the **South Pole (S)**.

> **Unbreakable Pairs:** You can never have a magnet with just one pole! If you cut a bar magnet in half, you do not get one North magnet and one South magnet. Instead, you get two smaller magnets, each with its own new North and South poles!

slides.title: Finding Directions with Magnets
slides.content:
# Finding Directions - The Magnetic Compass

For centuries, travelers, sailors, and explorers used the special property of freely suspended magnets to find their way across oceans and deserts.

## The Directive Property:
- A freely suspended magnet always comes to rest in the **North-South direction**.
- Ancient travelers used natural magnets (lodestone) suspended by a string to find directions when there were no landmarks.

## The Magnetic Compass:
- Later on, a device was developed based on this property, called a **compass**.
- A compass is a small glass-covered box with a magnetized needle inside.
- The needle is pivoted on a pin so it can rotate freely.
- **How it works:** 
  1. The magnetic needle always aligns itself to point North-South.
  2. The North pole of the needle is usually painted red to easily identify it.
  3. The compass has a dial with directions (North, South, East, West) marked on it.
  4. To find a direction, you place the compass flat and rotate the box until the 'N' mark aligns with the red tip of the needle. Now you know exactly where all the directions are!

## Why Does It Point North?
- The Earth behaves as if it has a giant bar magnet buried deep inside it.
- The Earth's magnetic South pole is located near the Geographic North pole.
- Since opposite poles attract, the North pole of the compass needle is pulled towards the Geographic North!

> **Modern Navigation:** Today we use GPS on our phones, but ships and airplanes still carry magnetic compasses as a reliable backup that doesn't need batteries to point North!

slides.title: Attraction and Repulsion
slides.content:
# Attraction and Repulsion - Magnetic Rules

What happens when you bring two magnets close to each other? They either pull together or push apart!

## The Rule of Poles:
Just like electrical charges, magnetic poles follow a simple rule:

### 1. Like Poles Repel (Push Away)
- Bring the **North** pole of one magnet near the **North** pole of another magnet. They will push each other away. You can feel an invisible force resisting you!
- Bring the **South** pole near the **South** pole. They will also repel.

### 2. Unlike Poles Attract (Pull Together)
- Bring the **North** pole of one magnet near the **South** pole of another. They will instantly pull together and stick tight!

## Repulsion is the Sure Test of a Magnet!
- How do you know if a piece of metal is a magnet or just a normal piece of iron?
- A magnet will **attract** a piece of iron.
- A magnet will also **attract** the opposite pole of another magnet.
- So, attraction doesn't prove an object is a magnet (it could just be iron).
- BUT, only two magnets can **repel** each other (when like poles face each other).
- Therefore, **repulsion is the sure test of magnetism!**

## Losing Magnetic Properties:
Magnets are powerful, but they can lose their "magic" if not treated properly. A magnet becomes weaker if:
- It is **heated** over a flame.
- It is **hit hard** with a hammer.
- It is **dropped** from a height repeatedly.
- It is not stored properly (magnets should be stored in pairs with unlike poles on the same side, separated by a piece of wood, and with soft iron pieces across their ends).

> **Floating Trains:** Maglev (Magnetic Levitation) trains use the power of magnetic repulsion to float above the tracks. Because they don't touch the tracks, there is no friction, allowing them to travel at incredible speeds over 500 km/h!

slides.title: Summary and Key Points
slides.content:
# Summary: Magnets

## Key Concepts:
- **Magnetite** is a natural magnet discovered in ancient times.
- **Artificial magnets** are made by humans in various shapes (bar, horseshoe, cylindrical).

## Materials:
- **Magnetic Materials:** Attracted by magnets (Iron, Nickel, Cobalt).
- **Non-Magnetic Materials:** Not attracted by magnets (Wood, plastic, aluminum, copper).

## Properties of Magnets:
- **Poles:** The force is strongest at the ends, called poles. Every magnet has a North (N) and South (S) pole. You cannot isolate a single pole.
- **Directional Property:** A freely suspended magnet always aligns in the North-South direction. This is used in making a **magnetic compass**.
- **Interaction:** 
  - **Unlike poles ATTRACT** (North pulls South).
  - **Like poles REPEL** (North pushes North, South pushes South).

## Care of Magnets:
- Magnets lose their power if heated, hammered, or dropped.
- They must be stored carefully using magnetic keepers.

> **Congratulations!** You now understand the invisible force of magnetism. You know how compasses guide explorers and the rules that make magnets attract and repel!
